items.followUp: Why does atomic radius generally decrease from left to right across a period?

rubric.why: Identifies the increasing nuclear attraction across a period.
rubric.description: Nuclear charge or effective nuclear charge increases from left to right.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that nuclear charge/effective nuclear charge increases across the period.

rubric.why: Explains that the stronger attraction makes electron removal more difficult.
rubric.description: The outer electron is held more strongly, so more energy is required to remove it.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking stronger attraction or decreasing atomic radius to increased ionization energy.

modelAnswer: From left to right in a period, nuclear charge increases while shielding changes very little.
The outer electrons are attracted more strongly and held closer to the nucleus, so more energy is needed to remove an electron.

items.followUp: Name the elements in the third period of the periodic table.

rubric.why: Checks identification of the first four elements of the second period.
rubric.description: Names or symbols for lithium, beryllium, boron and carbon.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark when all four elements are correctly named or symbolized.

rubric.why: Checks identification of the remaining four elements of the second period.
rubric.description: Names or symbols for nitrogen, oxygen, fluorine and neon.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark when all four elements are correctly named or symbolized.

modelAnswer: The elements in the second period are lithium (Li), beryllium (Be), boron (B), carbon (C), nitrogen (N), oxygen (O), fluorine (F) and neon (Ne).

items.followUp: Why do atoms gain, lose or share electrons when forming chemical bonds?

rubric.why: States the stability that atoms seek by reacting.
rubric.description: Atoms react to achieve a stable electronic configuration, usually like that of a noble gas.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that atoms seek a stable outer shell or noble-gas configuration.

rubric.why: Identifies how a stable outer shell is achieved.
rubric.description: Atoms complete their outermost shell by gaining, losing or sharing electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning a complete outer shell/duplet/octet or the relevant electron transfer or sharing.

modelAnswer: Atoms react to attain a stable electronic configuration, usually like that of a noble gas.
They do so by gaining, losing or sharing electrons to complete their outermost shell.

items.followUp: Why is ice less dense than liquid water?

rubric.why: Describes the open arrangement of water molecules in ice.
rubric.description: Hydrogen bonding forms an open cage-like structure in ice.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the open, cage-like structure formed in ice.

rubric.why: Connects the structure to the reason ice floats.
rubric.description: The open structure gives ice a lower density than liquid water, so it floats.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that ice is less dense than water or explaining this by its larger volume for the same mass.

modelAnswer: In ice, hydrogen bonds hold water molecules in an open cage-like structure.
This makes ice less dense than liquid water, so ice floats on water.

items.followUp: Why do ionic compounds generally have high melting points?

rubric.why: Identifies the strong forces holding the ions together.
rubric.description: Strong electrostatic forces of attraction exist between oppositely charged ions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that oppositely charged ions are held by strong electrostatic attraction.

rubric.why: Explains why ionic compounds form solids.
rubric.description: The ions are held in fixed positions in a crystal lattice, making the compound solid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning the fixed lattice arrangement or that substantial energy is needed to separate the ions.

modelAnswer: Ionic compounds contain oppositely charged ions held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction.
The ions occupy fixed positions in a crystal lattice, so the compounds are solids.

items.followUp: In which form does sulphur exist at 110 °C?

rubric.why: Checks the correct allotrope at the stated temperature.
rubric.description: Sulphur exists as monoclinic sulphur at 100 °C.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying monoclinic sulphur.

rubric.why: Confirms the temperature lies in the monoclinic form's stability range.
rubric.description: 100 °C is above the transition temperature of about 96 °C and below the melting point of about 119 °C.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving the relevant temperature range or correctly placing 100 °C within it.

modelAnswer: Sulphur exists as monoclinic sulphur at 100 °C.
This is because 100 °C lies between its transition temperature (about 96 °C) and melting point (about 119 °C).

items.followUp: Define diffusion in liquids and give one example.

rubric.why: Checks the meaning of diffusion in gases.
rubric.description: Diffusion is the spontaneous intermixing of gas particles due to their random motion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the spontaneous intermixing or spreading of gas particles.

rubric.why: Checks whether the student can give a relevant example.
rubric.description: An example is the smell of perfume or ammonia spreading through a room.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid example of a gas spreading and mixing.

modelAnswer: Diffusion in gases is the spontaneous intermixing of gas particles due to their random motion.
For example, the smell of perfume spreads through a room.

items.followUp: Why should a bottle of paint be shaken or stirred before use?

rubric.why: Identifies what happens to paint when left standing.
rubric.description: Solid pigment particles settle out of the liquid on standing.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the solid particles/pigment settle or sink when paint is left undisturbed.

rubric.why: Explains the purpose of stirring before use.
rubric.description: Stirring redistributes the settled particles to make the paint uniform.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that stirring redistributes or mixes the particles evenly.

modelAnswer: Paint contains solid pigment particles dispersed in a liquid, and these particles settle on standing.
We stir the paint to redisperse the particles and make the paint uniform before use.
